passage: At the school hobby club, trading card day was noisy. Eshaan, ten, laid out his spare cards and put a note next to his gold dragon card: "Ten cards only!" Sarika checked the club's trading list. "Dragons are worth three. Everyone knows that." "Not mine," Eshaan said. "Mine is special. I've had it since class three." Irawati offered four cards, then five. Eshaan shook his head. "You're trying to cheat me." By the end of the hour everyone had traded except Eshaan, who sat with his dragon and a sour face. "Nobody here knows what it's worth," he muttered.

qa.q: What does the club's trading list say dragons are worth?
qa.a: Dragons are worth three cards.

qa.q: Why does Eshaan think Irawati is trying to cheat him?
qa.a: Eshaan feels suspicious because the dragon is his and he has had it since class three, so it seems worth much more to him. A fair offer then feels like a trick.

qa.q: What could Eshaan ask himself before the next trading day?
qa.a: He could ask how many cards he would give to get that dragon from someone else; if the answer is three, that is probably a fair price.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel after offering five cards and being called a cheat?
qa.a: Irawati may feel hurt and confused, since five was already more than the list said.

grounding: Shows a boy demanding far more than his card is worth because it is his, and thinking others are cheating when they won't pay.

passage: I'm Gurleen, Kishore's elder sister, and I watched my brother try to sell his old cricket cards on our building's terrace. He had a stack of doubles. The other kids offered one rupee each, which is what they cost in the shop's mixed packets. Kishore asked for five. "These are from my collection," he said, as if that made them gold. Nobody paid. When the kids walked off, he told me they were all cheats who didn't understand value. Later I saw him counting the same cards in his room, very carefully. I'm not sure if he was upset or just stubborn.

qa.q: How much did the other kids offer for each card?
qa.a: The other kids offered one rupee each.

qa.q: Why did Kishore think the other kids were cheats?
qa.a: The cards felt valuable to him because they were his, so a fair price seemed like an insult rather than what buyers usually pay.

qa.q: How could Gurleen help her brother set a fair price next time?
qa.a: Gurleen could ask him how much he would pay for someone else's doubles, and suggest checking the shop price before asking.

qa.q: How might the kids who walked off see Kishore's price?
qa.a: They probably thought five rupees was silly for cards they could get from the shop for one, and didn't feel they were cheating anyone.

grounding: Shows a boy asking far more for his cards than buyers will pay because they are his, and calling the buyers cheats.

passage:
Monday: Chetan bought a shiny football card from the stationery shop for two rupees. It was just a card.
Wednesday: Leela wanted it for her album. "I'll give you three rupees." Chetan laughed. "Ten. It's mine now, and it's shiny." Leela said the shop had a whole box. "Then they're cheating people," Chetan said.
Saturday: The shop still had the box. Leela bought one for two rupees. Chetan watched her stick it in her album and felt strangely annoyed. His own card, still unsold, sat in his pocket, a little bent now.

qa.q: How much did Chetan pay for the football card?
qa.a: Chetan paid two rupees for it.

qa.q: Why did Chetan feel strangely annoyed on Saturday?
qa.a: He had valued the card at ten because it was his, and seeing Leela get the same card for two showed his price was only in his head.

qa.q: What could Chetan try the next time someone wants to buy something of his?
qa.a: He could check what the same thing costs in the shop and ask himself whether he'd pay his own price, then offer a fair deal.

qa.q: How might Leela see the whole thing?
qa.a: Leela probably thought three rupees was generous, and found it simple to buy her own card from the shop instead.

grounding: Shows a boy pricing an ordinary card far above its worth once he owns it and blaming the shop, while a buyer gets the same card cheaply.

passage: Swati, you want to know why your Pappu Nana and I didn't talk for a week in 1966? Let your Neelam Dadi tell you. He was ten, I was eight, and he loved one cricket card: a bowler in mid-jump, with a torn corner. In our Meerut lane any card was worth two marbles, three at most. Pappu wanted ten. "It's worth more because it's mine," he said. None of the boys would pay. He came home furious. "They're all cheating me!" I said, "Bhaiya, would you give ten marbles for Bunty's card?" "Of course not, his is ordinary." I laughed, and he stopped talking to me. He never sold it. It's still in his tin box. He showed it to you last Diwali, remember?

qa.q: How many marbles did Pappu want for his card?
qa.a: Ten marbles.

qa.q: Why did Pappu think the other boys were cheating him?
qa.a: Pappu felt furious because the card felt very special as his, so offers of two or three marbles seemed unfair. He couldn't see that to them it was an ordinary card.

qa.q: What question did young Neelam ask, and how could it have helped Pappu?
qa.a: She asked if he would give ten marbles for Bunty's card. If he had thought about it, he might have seen that buyers and owners value the same thing very differently.

qa.q: How might the other boys in the lane have seen Pappu's price?
qa.a: They probably thought ten marbles was silly for a torn card and may have been annoyed at being called cheats.

grounding: A grandmother recalls her brother as a boy who demanded far more for his card because it was his, and thought the others were cheating.

passage: The school bus left in six minutes, and the card swap on the back benches was ending. Uday, eleven, held up his silver goalkeeper card. "Fifty rupees, or five cards." His classmate Harsha laughed. "Those are twenty. I'll give you twenty." "Twenty? It's mine. I've had it since Class 4." "It's the same card the stationery shop sells." The driver honked. Two more boys offered fifteen and twenty. "You're all cheating," Uday said, face hot. Harsha shrugged and got on the bus. Uday climbed on last, card in hand. Halfway home he thought: if it were Harsha's card, would I pay fifty? He didn't like the answer. He put the card in his pencil box and said nothing.

qa.q: How much did Harsha offer for the silver goalkeeper card?
qa.a: I'll give you twenty.

qa.q: Why did Uday feel the others were cheating him?
qa.a: He had owned the card since Class 4, so it felt worth much more to him. The buyers only saw an ordinary shop card, and he took their lower offers as unfair.

qa.q: What question did Uday ask himself on the bus, and how could it help him next time?
qa.a: Whether he would pay fifty if it were Harsha's card. Asking this before setting a price could help him see the gap between what owners and buyers think.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Uday calling everyone cheats?
qa.a: Harsha probably thinks it's a bit unfair and silly, since twenty is the normal price, and just shrugs it off rather than arguing.

grounding: A boy rushing for the bus demands far more for his card because it is his, and accuses buyers of cheating when they won't pay.
